segments.narration: Spy satellites caught a 92-metre machine the CIA said couldn't fly. Kaspiysk harbour, on the Caspian Sea, late 1960s. Low over the water, in plain sight.
Ten jet engines. Five hundred and forty-four tonnes loaded. A wingspan barely a third of the hull's length.
So how does half a thousand tonnes stay up on stubs like that? Analysts filed it as KASP-A and argued.
It rode a cushion of its own trapped air, metres above the surface. A ground-effect craft, designed by Rostislav Alexeyev. Soviet engineers called it an ekranoplan.
First flight, October 1966. For twenty-two years nothing bigger flew anywhere, until pilot error dropped it into the Caspian in 1980.
